moduleTitle: Skipping a Process or a Stage
learningObjectives: Configure a Condition on a Process or Stage to control whether it runs in a given Case.
Distinguish the default run behavior of Processes and Stages and when each is appropriate to override.

topics.title: Conditional execution of processes and stages

studyGuide.sectionTitle: Conditional Execution of Processes and Stages

elements.description: Define conditions to control whether a Process or Stage runs in a Case. A condition consists of a property, an operator, and a value — evaluated at runtime against Case data.

elements.text: Think of an optional checklist section: the configured condition decides whether it applies to this Case. Check the business criterion explicitly; skipping work is not a blanket exemption from other requirements or a user’s arbitrary choice.

elements.description: In the described Stage configuration, the default is Never. A configured true skip condition bypasses Stage entry and the work that would start there. This is not a claim about cancelling work already started or every possible navigation mechanism.

By default, Processes ALWAYS start. To make a Process conditional, select the Process in the Case Life Cycle and configure a run condition. When the condition is not met, that specific Process is skipped.

The source example requires both Was a party injured = Yes and Expense total > USD50. Its condition is a conjunction. Do not generalize that example into a claim that Pega cannot represent OR logic or that every condition editor has the same controls.

The described App Studio procedure configures the selected Stage or Process in the Case Life Cycle properties panel. An inline field/comparator/value comparison does not require users to author a separate Rule; reusable conditions and their editors are distinct configurations.

elements.caption: Stage skip and Process start conditions have different polarity. This diagram describes entry/start checks, not retroactive cancellation of active work.

examPitfalls.title: Stage default = 'never skipped'; Process default = 'always starts'
examPitfalls.trapDescription: The reviewed defaults are Stage Never skipped and Process Always starts. These settings describe the conditional entry/start behavior, not a guarantee that every Case visits every Stage regardless of navigation.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: Stage = NEVER skipped (skip condition needed to bypass). Process = ALWAYS starts (run condition needed to restrict). Different defaults, different condition types.

examPitfalls.title: Stage condition = skip trigger; Process condition = run trigger
examPitfalls.trapDescription: Questions ask what a condition on a Stage does vs. a condition on a Process. Candidates say both define when the element 'should run.' A Stage condition defines WHEN to SKIP the Stage (evaluated on entry); a Process condition defines WHEN to RUN the Process — opposite logic.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: Stage: configure a SKIP condition (condition = true → Stage skipped). Process: configure a RUN/START condition (condition = false → Process skipped).

examPitfalls.title: Read the conjunction in the configured example
examPitfalls.trapDescription: The source’s injury/expense example explicitly requires both criteria. It does not establish that all possible condition editors forbid disjunction.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: For the stated AND example, both must match. For other requirements, inspect and configure the actual expression or reusable condition.

examPitfalls.title: Skipping a Stage bypasses ALL Processes within it
examPitfalls.trapDescription: A skipped Stage does not start its contained work through that Stage entry. Do not confuse this with a requirement to terminate existing work already running elsewhere.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: Skipping a Stage skips everything within it. Skipping a Process only affects that one Process — the Stage and other Processes continue.

examPitfalls.title: No separate Rule form — conditions configured inline in Case Life Cycle
examPitfalls.trapDescription: Use the selected Stage/Process panel for the described inline comparison. A separate Rule is not required for this example, but that does not prohibit reusable conditions in other configurations.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: Select the Stage or Process directly in the Case Life Cycle and configure the condition in its properties panel. No separate Rule form is needed.

examPitfalls.title: Conditions evaluate at runtime — not at design time
examPitfalls.trapDescription: Questions ask when skip/run conditions are evaluated. Candidates say 'when the Case Type is saved.' Conditions evaluate at RUNTIME when the case flow reaches that Stage or Process — never at design time or app save time.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: Conditions evaluate at runtime when the Case reaches the Stage or Process, using current Case field values. Each Case instance can have a different outcome.

examPitfalls.title: Stage skip and Process skip are independent
examPitfalls.trapDescription: A question asks whether skipping a Stage also applies the Stage's skip logic to its individual Processes. Candidates say yes. Stage skip and Process skip are independent — each is configured and evaluated separately. Skipping a Stage bypasses all Processes by containment, not by applying Process skip logic.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: A false Process start condition skips that Process; it does not copy or replace a Stage skip condition. Other Stage navigation remains a separate concern.

practiceQuiz.scenario: A 'Personal Injury Assessment' Stage has no skip condition configured. What happens when a Case reaches this Stage?

options.text: With the described default Never skip setting, it is not bypassed by a Stage skip condition
The Stage is skipped until a run condition is explicitly set to true
The Stage runs only if the previous Stage completed without errors
The Stage is skipped by default and must be activated per Case

practiceQuiz.hint: Recall the default behavior of a Stage that has no skip condition configured.
practiceQuiz.rationale: The reviewed default does not apply a Stage skip condition. That does not mean every Case must visit this Stage regardless of lifecycle navigation or resolution.

optionExplanations.A: Never skip is the described default criterion; it does not force visiting this Stage under every possible lifecycle path.
optionExplanations.B: The reviewed Stage setting is a skip trigger, not an initially false run condition requiring manual enablement.
optionExplanations.C: An error-free previous Stage is not an extra comparison in the described default skip setting.
optionExplanations.D: The topic does not describe default per-Case manual activation; the Stage skip setting starts at Never.

practiceQuiz.scenario: A 'File Injury Claim' Process has no run condition. What is its default behavior?

options.text: The Process always starts every time the Case reaches it
The Process never starts until a run condition evaluates to true
The Process runs once, then requires manual re-activation
The Process inherits the skip condition of its parent Stage

practiceQuiz.hint: Recall the default behavior of a Process that has no run condition configured.
practiceQuiz.rationale: Always starts is the reviewed Process default. To restrict entry, configure its start condition; this is distinct from a Stage skip condition and is not expressed as a Process Skip trigger in this example.

optionExplanations.A: Always starts is the default when processing reaches the configured start point, subject to the containing lifecycle context.
optionExplanations.B: A mandatory true condition before any Process can start contradicts the reviewed Always starts default.
optionExplanations.C: A one-time manual reactivation rule is not the default Process-start behavior described in this topic.
optionExplanations.D: The Process criterion does not inherit the Stage’s skip expression; skipping Stage entry prevents contained work by context.

practiceQuiz.scenario: Using the inline App Studio procedure described in the topic, how do you configure Medical Review to skip when Injury severity = None?

options.text: Select the 'Medical Review' Stage in the Case Life Cycle → set skip condition: Injury severity = None
Create a When Rule in Dev Studio named 'No Injury' → attach it to the Stage Rule form
Add a Decision shape before the Stage → route to the next Stage when condition is true
Configure each Process in the Stage with an individual run condition

practiceQuiz.hint: Stage skip conditions are set inline — select the Stage in the Case Life Cycle.
practiceQuiz.rationale: Select the Stage and configure its skip comparison in the Case Life Cycle panel. The question asks for this inline procedure; alternative navigation or reusable Rule patterns are not asserted impossible.

optionExplanations.A: This directly follows the topic’s inline Stage-panel procedure and supplies the requested field comparison.
optionExplanations.B: The question requests inline configuration, not separate Rule authoring; a reusable condition is a distinct design option.
optionExplanations.C: Decision-driven navigation is a different pattern from configuring the Stage’s own skip panel in this procedure.
optionExplanations.D: Individual Process criteria do not configure the Stage-level skip comparison requested by the scenario.

practiceQuiz.scenario: A Process must run only when 'Was a party injured' = Yes AND 'Expense total' > USD50. Both conditions are added. When does the Process run?

options.text: Only when BOTH conditions are simultaneously true
When EITHER condition is true
When the first condition is true — the second is only checked if the first fails
The user selects which condition to apply at runtime

practiceQuiz.hint: When multiple run conditions are added to a Process, what logical operator combines them?
practiceQuiz.rationale: The scenario expressly requires the conjunction of the two criteria, so both must match. This is about the configured logical expression, not a universal limit on all condition-building interfaces.

optionExplanations.A: Both comparisons must match the expressly stated AND requirement; this explains this configuration’s outcome.
optionExplanations.B: Either criterion sufficing would be OR rather than the requested conjunctive injury-and-expense test.
optionExplanations.C: Checking the second only after the first fails does not implement the requirement for both to be true.
optionExplanations.D: The configured expression, not an arbitrary user choice of criteria, determines whether this Process starts.

practiceQuiz.scenario: A Stage's skip condition evaluates to true. What happens to the Processes inside that Stage?

options.text: All Processes within the Stage are bypassed — the entire Stage is skipped
Only the first Process is skipped; the remaining Processes still execute
The Processes run but all Assignments are auto-completed
A user must manually confirm whether to skip each Process

practiceQuiz.hint: Skipping a Stage = skipping everything inside it.
practiceQuiz.rationale: Stage-level and Process-level skip conditions are independent. A Stage skip bypasses the entire Stage including all Processes. A Process skip only bypasses that Process within an otherwise active Stage.

optionExplanations.A: Bypassing Stage entry bypasses starting its contained work through that entry; it does not retroactively terminate unrelated active work.
optionExplanations.B: The condition applies at Stage scope rather than selecting only the first contained Process to skip.
optionExplanations.C: Skipping entry is not automatic completion of every Assignment; that would be a different processing mechanism.
optionExplanations.D: The described condition is evaluated against Case data rather than requiring users to confirm each Process skip.

practiceQuiz.scenario: Inside an entered Stage with other work to perform, Collect Additional Documents has a false start condition. Does that alone skip the parent Stage?

options.text: The Stage continues running — other Processes in the Stage are unaffected
The Stage is also skipped — skipping a Process automatically skips its parent Stage
The Stage is paused until the Process condition changes
The Stage generates a guardrail violation for the skipped Process

practiceQuiz.hint: Stage-level skip and Process-level skip are independently configured and can coexist.
practiceQuiz.rationale: The false Process start condition bypasses that Process. It does not itself change the Stage’s entry configuration or the conditions of other Processes.

optionExplanations.A: That Process condition alone does not skip the parent Stage or alter other Processes’ own start criteria.
optionExplanations.B: The parent is not automatically skipped merely because one contained Process does not start.
optionExplanations.C: False start logic bypasses the Process; it is not a waiting condition for future field changes.
optionExplanations.D: Conditional omission is an intended pattern, not automatically a guardrail violation merely because it occurs.

practiceQuiz.scenario: What three parts make up the inline field comparison illustrated for a Stage skip or Process start condition?

options.text: A property, an operator, and a value
A When Rule name, a result type, and a target Stage
A field name, a Data Page reference, and a fallback value
A Decision table, a column selector, and an expected result

practiceQuiz.hint: Identify the field being compared, the comparison and its target value.
practiceQuiz.rationale: The illustrated comparison has a field/property, comparator/operator and value. This is not a universal definition that every When Rule or logical expression must contain exactly one comparison.

optionExplanations.A: The inline comparison names its input, comparison operator and target; compound expressions can combine such comparisons.
optionExplanations.B: A target Stage and result type are not the three components of the illustrated field comparison.
optionExplanations.C: A Data Page and fallback may support other data behavior, but they are not the illustrated comparison components.
optionExplanations.D: Table columns and expected output describe another decision structure, not this inline field comparison.

practiceQuiz.scenario: A Pega developer is deciding whether to add Skip or Run conditions to a set of Stages and Processes in a Claims Case and wants to understand what happens if no conditions are configured. Which TWO statements correctly describe the default execution behavior of Stages and Processes in Pega?

options.text: Stages are never skipped by default
Processes always start by default
Stages always require an explicit run condition to execute
Processes are skipped by default and need activation

practiceQuiz.hint: Stage default = never skipped. Process default = always starts.
practiceQuiz.rationale: The reviewed defaults distinguish Stage Never skipped from Process Always starts. They do not require explicit enabling criteria before the relevant entry/start point.

optionExplanations.A: The Stage’s reviewed default is Never skipped by this criterion, rather than requiring an explicit true run comparison.
optionExplanations.B: The Process’s reviewed default is Always starts at its relevant start point, not default omission pending activation.
optionExplanations.C: An explicit run condition is not required by the stated default Stage configuration.
optionExplanations.D: Processes are not skipped pending activation by default; the reviewed start setting is Always starts.

practiceQuiz.scenario: An SA configures a Skip Condition on a Review Stage that evaluates the claim amount property. A developer asks at what point during Case processing this condition is actually evaluated to determine whether the Stage should be skipped. When are skip and run conditions evaluated in a Pega Case?

options.text: At runtime, when the Case reaches the Stage or Process — using current Case field values
At design time, when the Case Type is saved in App Studio
Once at Case creation — conditions are not re-evaluated after the Case opens
During a nightly batch process that pre-computes Case routing

practiceQuiz.hint: Conditions use live Case data — they must be evaluated at runtime.
practiceQuiz.rationale: Conditions evaluate at runtime when the Case reaches the configured Stage or Process. Each Case instance evaluates independently based on its own data. B, C, D all describe incorrect timing.

optionExplanations.A: The runtime criterion compares the Case’s data at the relevant entry/start point; different Cases can satisfy it differently.
optionExplanations.B: Saving a Case Type configures the criterion; it does not determine every future Case’s input-dependent outcome.
optionExplanations.C: A universal creation-time-only evaluation would ignore data available at the later entry/start point described here.
optionExplanations.D: The topic does not use nightly precomputed routing to evaluate this entry/start criterion.

practiceQuiz.scenario: The source’s two-condition example combines criteria with AND. If Claim type = Auto and Claim type = Property were combined that same way for a single-valued field, would this express Auto OR Property?

options.text: No — that conjunction requires both comparisons; the requested alternative needs an OR expression instead
Yes — an AND expression means either comparison is enough
Yes — the same single-valued field automatically has both category values at once
No — only one condition per Process is supported

practiceQuiz.hint: Reason about the stated AND expression, not assumed editor limitations.
practiceQuiz.rationale: A single-valued category cannot equal two distinct values at once. The specified conjunction is not the requested disjunction; configure the intended logic rather than assuming that Pega universally forbids OR.

optionExplanations.A: The explicitly stated conjunction does not express either category; an alternative expression must represent the requested disjunction.
optionExplanations.B: AND is not OR; satisfying one of two comparisons does not satisfy their conjunction.
optionExplanations.C: A single-valued category cannot equal Auto and Property at once; it does not become multi-valued implicitly.
optionExplanations.D: The example supports multiple comparisons, so rejecting it because only one comparison is allowed is incorrect.

practiceQuiz.scenario: In the documented automobile-accident example, which comparison makes File personal injury claim run only for a reported injury?

options.text: 'Was a party injured' = Yes
'Accident type' = Personal injury
'Claim status' ≠ Closed
'Process type' = Personal injury claim

practiceQuiz.hint: The Pega Academy example uses 'Was a party injured' = Yes.
practiceQuiz.rationale: 'Was a party injured' = Yes is the documented Pega Academy example for this Process condition. B, C, D reference fields or values not in the documented example.

optionExplanations.A: This is the actual injury comparison in the source example; the question asks about that documented configuration.
optionExplanations.B: An alternative schema could use other fields, but this is not the comparison in the documented example requested here.
optionExplanations.C: A nonclosed claim does not by itself establish that a party was injured in the stated example.
optionExplanations.D: Naming the Process describes workflow configuration rather than the injury field value used by the example.

practiceQuiz.scenario: An entered Stage has other work to perform, and one Process start condition skips that Process. Must its parent Stage skip condition change solely for that reason?

options.text: No — Process start and Stage skip criteria are separate; the Process condition alone does not require a Stage condition change
Yes — the Stage skip condition must be updated to reflect the Process being skipped
Yes — skipping a Process invalidates the Stage's default run behavior
Only if the skipped Process is the first Process in the Stage

practiceQuiz.hint: Process skip has no effect on the parent Stage.
practiceQuiz.rationale: The Process criterion does not require changing the Stage criterion merely because this Process did not start. This is not a guarantee about every later navigation or lifecycle outcome.

optionExplanations.A: The Process condition alone does not require replacing or editing the separate Stage entry criterion.
optionExplanations.B: A Process not starting does not by itself require a mirrored Stage skip expression; they apply at different scopes.
optionExplanations.C: Conditional Process omission does not invalidate the Stage’s configured entry behavior merely because it happened.
optionExplanations.D: First-Process position does not create the mandatory Stage-condition update proposed by this option.

practiceQuiz.scenario: Which TWO statements describe the inline configuration for skipping a Stage when Claim amount is below $1,000?

options.text: Configure the Stage’s skip comparison for Claim amount below $1,000
A true skip comparison at entry bypasses the Stage; it does not require a second separately authored Rule for this inline example
A separate Declare Expression is mandatory before this inline Stage comparison can be configured
A separate low-value-Claims Case Type is required instead of configuring the existing Stage condition

practiceQuiz.hint: Identify the configuration location and the true-skip behavior; avoid inventing a second required artifact.
practiceQuiz.rationale: The Stage panel can hold the inline comparison, and true skip logic bypasses entry. A separately authored When Rule or Declare Expression is not a second mandatory artifact for this example.

optionExplanations.A: The inline Stage skip comparison directly states the required amount threshold in the Stage configuration context.
optionExplanations.B: True skip logic bypasses entry; a second separately authored Rule is not necessary for this inline comparison.
optionExplanations.C: A separate Boolean Declare Expression is not required merely to compare the available amount field inline.
optionExplanations.D: A new Case Type is not necessary to conditionally omit a Stage within the existing lifecycle.

practiceQuiz.scenario: A Pega developer asks about the behavior of a Process configured with a run condition. Which TWO statements correctly describe what happens when a run condition is applied to a Process?

options.text: If the run condition evaluates to false at runtime, the entire Process is skipped and none of its Steps execute
The start condition can compare an available Case field at runtime to decide whether this Process starts
A false run condition on a Process automatically skips the entire Stage that contains it
Run conditions on Processes can only be configured in Dev Studio — App Studio does not support them

practiceQuiz.hint: False skips this Process; the comparison uses available Case data in its configuration context.
practiceQuiz.rationale: A false start condition prevents that Process from starting. Available Case fields supply the comparison inputs; that is not a promise that arbitrary properties are exposed or that the parent Stage is skipped.

optionExplanations.A: At the start point, a false criterion prevents this Process’s work from starting; it is not retroactive cancellation.
optionExplanations.B: An available Case field supplies a runtime input; availability depends on configuration context rather than arbitrary-property access.
optionExplanations.C: False Process start logic does not automatically become a Stage-level skip trigger.
optionExplanations.D: The reviewed configuration is available through the Case Life Cycle; it is not exclusively a Dev Studio task.

quickRecap.value: NEVER skipped. Add a skip condition (property + operator + value) to bypass it. When condition = true → entire Stage and all Processes within it are skipped.
ALWAYS starts. Add a run condition to restrict execution. When condition = false → that Process is skipped.
The source’s injury-and-expense example uses AND. Inspect actual configured logic; do not infer a universal restriction on OR expressions.

quickRecap.key: Skipping a Stage vs. a Process
quickRecap.value: Stage skip → all Processes inside bypassed. Process skip → only that Process skipped; Stage and other Processes unaffected.
Select the Stage or Process in the Case Life Cycle to configure the described inline comparison; no second Rule is required for that example.
Runtime — evaluated when Case reaches the Stage or Process, using current Case field values.
'File personal injury claim' Process runs only when 'Was a party injured' = Yes (AND 'Expense total' > USD50 when a second condition is added).
